Hi everyone! I'm Marcin Bugaj. I've been learning Lean 4 and Mathlib, with a focus on inequalities and majorization theory. I just opened my first PR, https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/41898 - the majorization preorder on Fin n → ℝ and its T-transform (Robin Hood) decomposition.

Muirhead's inequality is ready too and will follow as a dependent PR on top of this one. Further ahead I also plan to add other characterizations of majorization - in particular via convex functions (Karamata's inequality) and related results on convex functions.

As it's my first contribution, I'd really appreciate feedback, including on file placement (Mathlib/Analysis/Convex/Majorization.lean), naming (Majorizes, ≺, TTransform), and whether the ≺ notation should stay scoped. Thanks!
cc @Bhavik Mehta who also implemented the majorization order
And @Frédéric Dupuis has an open PR for majorization already. I may have asked too much in review that it is stalled, but it could likely be easily recovered.

Hi, and thanks for the pointers! I've now looked at Frederic's PR #33406. Since both PRs define majorization, I'd like to avoid two parallel definitions, so I'd appreciate your guidance on how you'd like to reconcile them. My work contains the T-transform (Robin Hood) decomposition. That's complementary to the doubly-stochastic characterization already in #33406.

How would you suggest we reconcile the two?
#new members > Marcin Bugaj - introduction

I think we'll want the version in #33406 despite my comments on that PR about decreasing rearrangements. We will certainly want API for decreasing rearrangements too, but dealing with the Equivs back and forth is indeed painful. The version in #41898 has the immediate downside that it only works for Fin n, whereas #33406 works for Fintypes (and even if you want decreasing rearrangements, it still works for linearly ordered finite types).

Some comments about #41898:

  1. I would not have made docs#TTransform a structure, but rather a bare function taking as input (a b : n → ℝ) (k l : n) (t : ℝ), where n : Type*. In fact, I wouldn't have even forced the codomain to be ℝ (for example, maybe you want it to be ℚ or ℝ≥0 or ℝ≥0∞ sometimes, who knows at this point). And indeed, I maybe would have taken a b : n → M and t : R where M is an R-module. Side note: it's weird to call it a t-transform and then use lambda as your parameter.
  2. Using docs#Relation.ReflTransGen with RelatedByTTransform is not a bad idea necessarily, but it does lack the information about the number of t-transforms required, which is a bit unfortunate. Moreover, in scenarios where you want to work with t-transforms, it is often the case that you care about the explicit sequence of ts used. So I think it would be better to create a def which builds the sequence recursively. Then, if desired, the ReflTransGen version can be derived as an easy corollary.
  3. When dealing with majorization, especially using decreasing rearrangements, it's often very helpful for proofs to consider, given two antitone sequences a b : Fin n → R with a majorized by b, the nonnegative sequence δ : Fin n → R consisting of the partial sums of the difference. IIRC Marshall-Olkin-Arnold does this occasionally, but it's been several years since I looked carefully at that text.
So, I don't think we want #41898 as is, but certainly we will want some of the results you've proven there, in perhaps slightly different forms, after #33406 is merged.

It might be worth going for a more general definition of majorization (not to say anything about the lemmas for the n → M case). There's a generalization of Muirhead's inequality by Schulman where given a normed space V and (compact) measurable group G acting on V, majorization for a b : V means ∃ ν : Measure G, IsProbabilityMeasure ν ∧ a = ∫ g : G, g • b ∂ν.

I'm leaning towards the definition of "semigroup majorization" (but really "monoid majorization") in 14C of this book. Given a monoid M and acting on α, b : α majorizes a : α means ∃ m : M, a = m • b. For the n → M case, M would be docs#doublyStochastic and the action is matrix multiplication. For Schulman's generalization, M would be docs#MeasureTheory.ProbabilityMeasure with multiplication being docs#MeasureTheory.Measure.mconv and the action being what I have above. Maybe this could be called MonoidMajorize.

I was planning to revisit this at some point to try to formalise the definition that works for infinite sequences, but unfortunately I haven't had the time to do this yet, and I almost certainly won't be able to get to it before September. So feel free to disregard my previous PR and the topic and go ahead, I wouldn't want to slow things down.
